nameStory: This moth gets its name from the tufts of fuzzy hair (called tussocks) that cover its caterpillars, and its close relationship with milkweed plants. The caterpillars feast exclusively on milkweeds and dogbane, making milkweed patches their primary nursery grounds. It's also called the milkweed tiger moth for the bold, contrasting patterns typical of tiger moths.
description: The milkweed tussock moth is a medium-sized moth with distinctive markings that belongs to the tiger moth family. Adults have grayish wings with bold black and white patterns, while their famous caterpillars are covered in dense tufts of orange, black, and white fuzzy hairs. The moths are most commonly seen from mid-summer through late summer when they're actively feeding and mating. These moths have evolved a clever chemical defense system, storing toxins from their milkweed diet that make them unpalatable to predators.

idTips.label: Fuzzy caterpillars with colorful tufts
idTips.description: Look for densely hairy caterpillars with prominent tufts of orange, black, and white bristles that feel soft but slightly prickly to the touch - these distinctive 'tussocks' give the moth its name

idTips.label: Adult wing patterns
idTips.description: Gray wings marked with bold black spots and white patches, creating a striking tiger-like pattern that's easy to spot against tree bark or flowers

idTips.label: Milkweed association
idTips.description: Almost always found on or near milkweed plants and dogbane, where caterpillars feed and adults seek mates - if you see fuzzy caterpillars on milkweed, they're likely this species

idTips.label: Clicking sounds
idTips.description: Adults can produce ultrasonic clicking sounds with special organs called tymbals - while humans can't hear these, you might notice bats avoiding these moths

idTips.label: Defensive behavior
idTips.description: When disturbed, caterpillars curl up into a tight ball and may release a slight bitter smell from the toxins they've accumulated from eating milkweed

habitat: Found throughout New England in open areas where milkweeds grow, including fields, meadows, roadsides, and garden edges. They prefer sunny locations with common milkweed, swamp milkweed, or dogbane plants. You'll often spot them in disturbed areas, abandoned lots, and prairie-style plantings from sea level to moderate elevations.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, but activity is minimal. Look for overwintering pupae in leaf litter near milkweed patches.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity from mid to late summer when fuzzy caterpillars are most visible on milkweed plants and adults are actively flying and mating. This is the best time to spot both life stages.
seasonality.fall: Late caterpillars may still be feeding in early fall before pupating. Adults become scarce as they complete their life cycle and prepare for winter.
seasonality.winter: Pupae overwinter in cocoons hidden in leaf litter and soil. No active stages are visible above ground during the coldest months.

funFact: These moths are essentially flying chemical warfare units - they absorb heart-stopping toxins called cardiac glycosides from milkweed, then warn bats to stay away by clicking at them in ultrasonic frequencies, like a poisonous moth's version of a rattlesnake's rattle!
confusionNotes: The fuzzy caterpillars might be confused with woolly bear caterpillars, but milkweed tussock moth caterpillars have much more organized, tufted hair arrangements and are almost always found on milkweed plants. Remember: if it's fuzzy and on milkweed, it's likely a tussock moth.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called both a 'tiger moth' and 'tussock moth,' this species is actually in the family Erebidae, which includes many moths previously classified in separate families. The 'tiger' name refers to the bold patterns, while 'tussock' describes the caterpillar's hairy tufts - so both names capture different life stages of the same species.
compareHints: As the only Euchaetes species in New England, compare it with other tiger moths in the region. Unlike the more uniformly colored woolly bears or the larger cecropia moths, milkweed tussock moths have that distinctive combination of fuzzy, tufted caterpillars and gray-and-black patterned adults. Their exclusive relationship with milkweeds also sets them apart from most other moths in the area.
